plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 8: Further Applications of Trigonometry
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single-panel diagram of a right triangle drawn in the complex plane, with the horizontal axis labeled "Real" and the vertical axis labeled "Imaginary," each drawn as a thin double-headed arrow through the origin. A filled black dot sits in the first quadrant and is labeled "x + yi." A straight segment runs from the origin out to that dot and is labeled r; from the dot a vertical segment drops to the horizontal axis and is labeled y, and the horizontal leg from the origin to the foot of that drop is labeled x, closing the triangle with a right angle at the foot. The angle at the origin, between the positive real direction and the segment r, is marked with a small arc and labeled with the Greek letter theta. A heavier curved arc of constant radius sweeps through the labeled dot and carries arrowheads at both ends, one pointing left beyond the imaginary axis and the other pointing down beyond the real axis, tracing a circle centered at the origin. Laying the rectangular pair x and y and the polar pair r and theta on the same picture lets the reader read either description off the other. The drawing fixes r as the modulus, the distance from the origin to the point, and theta as the direction angle, the two quantities that make up the polar form of a complex number.

interactionPlan.concept: A complex number can be described either by rectangular coordinates x + yi or by polar coordinates r and θ, where r is distance from the origin and θ is the direction angle from the positive real axis.

interactions.label: θ angle
interactions.teaches: Changing θ rotates the point around a circle centered at the origin, showing that the angle determines direction while x and y update as projections.

interactions.label: r modulus
interactions.teaches: Changing r moves the point closer to or farther from the origin along the same direction, showing that r is the point's distance from the origin.

interactions.label: Coordinate labels
interactions.teaches: The same point can be read as rectangular coordinates x and y or as polar coordinates r and θ; the labels change, but the point does not.

demo_steps.title: See both coordinate descriptions
demo_steps.narration: The point is labeled as x + yi, while the same geometry also shows r as the distance from the origin and θ as the direction angle. Rectangular and polar form describe the same location.

demo_steps.title: Rotate the direction angle
demo_steps.narration: Drag θ and watch the point travel along a circular path. The radius stays fixed, but the horizontal and vertical legs change because x and y are projections of the rotating radius.

demo_steps.title: Change the modulus
demo_steps.narration: Now change r and notice that the point moves directly toward or away from the origin along the same ray. The circle grows or shrinks because r is the radius of that circle.

demo_steps.title: Compare labels for the same point
demo_steps.narration: Switch between rectangular and polar labels without moving the point. This shows that x + yi and the pair r, θ are two coordinate descriptions of one complex number.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Polar form replaces the rectangular projections x and y with the distance r and direction θ of the very same point in the complex plane.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean SVG-style complex plane with thin gray or black double-headed axes crossing at the origin. Draw the triangle and circular arc in dark blue, with a black point on the arc in the first quadrant for the default state. The horizontal leg extends from the origin to the point's vertical projection on the real axis, and the vertical leg rises to the point; include a small right-angle box at the projection foot. The radial segment should be visually strongest because it represents r. The large circular arc should be centered at the origin and pass through the point, with arrowheads at both ends as in the source figure. In rectangular label mode show x, y, and x + yi prominently; in polar label mode show r and θ prominently; in both mode show all labels without excessive clutter.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for theta: the learner drags the angle from the positive real axis, the point moves around the circular arc while x and y legs update, and the link between direction angle and rectangular coordinates becomes clear.
- Slider for r: the learner changes the modulus, the segment from the origin and the circle radius grow or shrink with the point, and r becomes visible as distance from the origin rather than a separate label.
- Toggle between rectangular and polar labels: the learner switches the displayed annotations from x and y to r and theta, the same point keeps its position while the labels change, and the equivalence between x + yi and polar form is emphasized.

authoredContext:
We review these relationships in the figure.

Triangle plotted in the complex plane (x axis is real, y axis is imaginary). Base is along the x/real axis, height is some y/imaginary value in Q 1, and hypotenuse r extends from origin to that point (x+yi) in Q 1. The angle at the origin is theta. There is an arc going through (x+yi).

We use the term modulus to represent the absolute value of a complex number, or the distance from the origin to the point (x,y). The modulus, then, is the same as r, the radius in polar form. We use θ to indicate the angle of direction (just as with polar coordinates). Substituting, we have

evaluation.notes: The generated figure captures the complex-number polar/rectangular construction with correct labels and useful controls, but the main construction is scaled too small and slightly crowded compared with the source.

Adjust the circular arc start/end angles and arrowhead placement so the upper-left and lower-right arrow positions match the source more closely.
Move the θ label and right-angle marker slightly apart, or enlarge the construction, to reduce crowding near the foot of the vertical projection.
Remove the extra origin dot unless it is intentionally part of the textbook figure.
